prop: The independence argument that rescued `Domain ⊆ Extent` transfers to a semantic mint-time verifier. `scope.rs` records that the comparison failed only because one author supplied both sides, and that what fixed it was making one side captured by the tool (extent, with deliberately no flag to type one in) and the other authored (the note). A claim's proposition is authored by the same hand; its cited facts' captured output was recorded by `look`/`run` under the same no-typed-input rule. So the two sides of a proposition-versus-captured-output comparison are independent by the same construction, not by the author's diligence.

`scope.rs` states its own residual gap in terms that name the semantic verifier's job: of the two overreaching facts that motivated it, it catches one, and the one it misses (F7, "mirrors the server's" over an extent covering only the client) is missed because the overreach names no location at all — "invisible to any check of this shape". Its rejected refinement is recorded with the same reason: naming a symbol the read code calls is normal while concluding about what that symbol does is the failure, and "those two are not distinguishable by string matching." A check that compares meaning rather than location is therefore aimed at a gap the existing check documents rather than at a new speculation.

The warning should be carried as a top-level `verify` OBJECT in the mint result, not a fourth array beside `attention` and `overlap`. `mcp.rs` establishes the array form for a reason that holds here — "the caller is a program, and a field it can branch on beats a string it has to notice" — but `attention` and `overlap` are derived per call from workspace state already on disk, so empty and absent mean the same thing for them. A verifier can fail to run, and "found nothing" must be distinguishable from "did not look". An object with a mandatory `status` field carrying exactly one of `ok`, `off`, `unavailable`, `timeout`, `unauthorized`, and a `findings` array that is meaningful only when `status` is `ok`, makes that distinction branchable; a bare array cannot express it.

The non-determinism of this check is measured, not merely theoretical, and the disclosure must be carried in the surface rather than left in documentation. The eval recorded that on identical input at temperature 0 the model's reasoning length swings 516..2000 tokens, and that draws reaching the token cap return `finish_reason=length` with content of length zero — so identical mints can produce different `verify` payloads, including a finding on one run and silence on the next. This is a real departure from `attention` and `overlap`, which are derived per call from workspace state already on disk and therefore repeat exactly. The `verify` object must therefore state its own model and a `deterministic: false` marker in every response, so a reader cannot infer parity with the two findings sitting beside it.

The eval settles which approach to build and settles nothing about whether to build it. It settles the approach: on 15 cases run 3 times, the one-call direct comparison caught 32/33 planted defects and left 12/12 sound claims alone at $0.0060, against 28/32 and 7/12 at $0.0532 for the three-call extract-then-judge pipeline — better on both axes at a ninth of the cost, so the pipeline hypothesis did not survive measurement. It settles nothing about value, by its own statement: the case set is small, self-authored and synthetic with no case taken from a real memo, one case was found mislabeled by the model disagreeing with it, and "Nothing here measures whether warning an author earlier removes a grounding round, which is the actual cost argument."

The extract-then-compare pipeline should remain selectable despite losing the measurement, because it holds one property the winner cannot have and that property is about auditability rather than accuracy: its findings are re-derivable by anyone holding the two extracted records, with no model in the loop, whereas the direct comparison's findings are not re-derivable without a model. Its accuracy numbers (17/30 caught, 11/12 left alone) were taken on the earlier 14-case set and so are not comparable with the 15-case columns, which means the case for keeping it must rest on that property and not on its score.

The environment-only rule for the API key needs one addition to `config.rs` and gets the rest for free. Free: there is no `verify.api_key` in the KEYS registry, and `set` resolves a key through `key_def` and refuses what is not there, listing `known_keys()` so the author is told what they could have written instead — so a key-shaped SETTING is already unwritable. The addition is at the value level: `verify.model`, being a string key, would accept a credential pasted into it, and the strict-when-set half of the asymmetry is the correct hook for a new `Accepts` rule that refuses a credential-shaped value. That refusal is legitimate under the no-heuristic-refusal doctrine because `set` already refuses on value shape by design, and refusing at write time cannot suppress a mint.

The verifier's settings may be added to `config.rs` only because each is visible in the output it affects, which is the module's own stated admission test: "every setting here must be visible in the output it affects ... A setting that could not be shown that way should not be added to this file." The proposed `verify` result object satisfies it by echoing status, model name and the non-determinism marker in every response, so a reader can tell which settings produced the result in front of them without opening a config file. The keys — `verify.enabled` (bool), `verify.model` (string), `verify.approach` (direct or pipeline), `verify.timeout_ms` (int) and `verify.verbs` (which mint verbs are checked) — are each one entry in the existing static KEYS registry with an `accepts` rule, live at the two existing scopes, and need no third scope.

Shipping this falsifies one of `lib.rs`'s two pinned whole-crate properties, and the correct replacement is a per-command row rather than a weakened sentence — which is what the module's own preamble already prescribes, having recorded that "a single sentence about the whole crate was wrong for months" and having restated the write list per command for exactly that reason. The property that breaks is "there are no network calls anywhere, which the dependency set enforces rather than the prose": once an HTTP client is linked, the dependency set no longer enforces anything and the sentence would be prose pretending to be an invariant. The replacement row names the reaching commands — `fact`, `claim` and `prose` may make one outbound call to the configured provider, and only when enabled with a key in the environment — and states that `check`, `brief`, `query`, `review`, `workspaces`, `render`, `record` and `config` make none. The crate's other pinned property, that nothing here ever executes a command named by a document, is untouched and is the reason `check` must not be a reaching command.

This finding belongs to neither of `report.rs`'s two partitions, and that is the answer rather than an evasion of the question. Both arrays are documented as the canonical category names of the MACHINE-CHECKED and HUMAN-OWED partitions of `check`'s output, built from a single enumerated source precisely so the scope strings and the `check` tool description cannot drift from what `check` does. A finding that is produced at mint time, never runs inside `check`, and never enters the record, memo, snapshot or evidence ledger is not a thing `check` can report; adding it to either array would make both partitions' scope strings assert coverage that `check` does not have. Its correct home is the mint result alone.

A workspace-local `verify.log` beside `refusals.log` is the right place for findings to persist, but `refusals.log` is the wrong sibling to imitate in one specific respect: it is an entry in SNAPSHOT_FILES and therefore ships into `<memo>.tetel/` with every render. A log of model output that shipped that way would put non-reproducible text into the snapshot, which is the one thing this design must not do. What makes the omission safe is that SNAPSHOT_FILES is an enumerated allowlist rather than a denylist — a new workspace file is withheld by default and ships only when someone adds a line with a justifying comment beside every other entry's. So `verify.log` is enforced out of the snapshot by construction, not by a promise, and its absence needs no new mechanism.

Latency is the binding constraint and it is larger than a per-record estimate suggests, because the unit that pays it is the tool call and not the record. In the largest memo on disk (tet47) the append-only logs carry 33 + 114 + 130 = 277 lines across facts, claims and prose, and 114 of those claim lines resolve to only 39 distinct claim ids — so roughly two thirds of claim traffic is revision. At the eval's observed per-call latency, verifying every line of that run costs tens of minutes of added wall-clock, while the money stays negligible. The design must therefore (a) commit the mint before the verifier runs, so a slow provider delays only the reply and never the record, (b) bound the wait with `verify.timeout_ms` and report `status: timeout` when it expires, and (c) skip the call entirely when a revision does not change the text being compared, which is where most of the volume is.

Only `claim` should be checked by default, with `fact` and `prose` available through `verify.verbs` but off. `claim` is the verb the eval actually measured — its cases imitate "the shape of a tetel claim and its captured evidence" — so it is the only one of the three whose accuracy numbers mean anything. `fact` is partly covered already, deterministically and for free, by the `scope` check, and the semantic residue it would add is real but is the smaller of the two halves `scope.rs` describes. `prose` is the highest-volume verb of the three in the largest memo measured (130 log lines against 114 for claims and 33 for facts), and comparing prose against claim propositions is a different comparison from the one measured, with no numbers behind it at all. Defaulting it on would spend the largest share of the latency budget on the least-evidenced comparison.

The modification surface is small and censused. `fact_result` has exactly one definition and two production call sites, both in src/mcp.rs — the "minted" and "revised" arms — so adding a `verify` key to that one builder covers both fact outcomes and touches no other production caller; the only other occurrences in the worktree are a same-named local binding in a test. On the config side, `known_keys` occurs twice in the whole worktree, both inside src/config.rs, and `Accepts` six times, also all inside src/config.rs, with a single variant in use. Adding the `verify.*` keys therefore means new registry entries, new `Accepts` variants and matching arms in `accepted` and its message formatter, with no consumer outside that module to update.

The degradation contract is format-level and total: every terminal state of the provider call maps to exactly one `verify.status` value, and no state maps to `ok` with an empty `findings` array unless the model returned a well-formed answer containing no finding. Disabled by config gives `off`; no key in the environment gives `unauthorized`; a transport failure or non-2xx gives `unavailable`; expiry of `verify.timeout_ms` gives `timeout`. An empty or truncated response body is `unavailable` and never `ok`, because the eval measured exactly that state — a draw reaching the token ceiling returns a zero-length body — and because the same eval's harness recorded scoring an error as an answer as one of the two defects that inflated its own results. In every non-`ok` state the mint has already committed, so the contract can never fail a mint or change an exit code.

A finding must name the failing clause and quote the captured evidence rather than assert a verdict, and the eval supplies the reason as a measured case rather than a worry. The three-call pipeline's false positives were all one failure mode — the extractor drops a binding and the judge cannot tell a dropped binding from an absent one — and the recorded instance is a finding that reported "the evidence contains no `pin` name or binding" against evidence whose lines 425-436 are the pin computation. That finding is a verdict: a recipient can only accept or ignore it. Had it named the clause it was judging and quoted the evidence lines it judged against, its wrongness would have been visible in one step to a reader with the memo in front of them. So each entry carries the quoted clause, the fact id and the quoted span it was compared against, and no confidence score — the recipient is usually an agent that will act on a warning, and a verdict invites compliance where a quotation invites checking.

The retrodiction test is runnable today on a corpus already on disk, and its shape is fixed by the file formats rather than chosen. Seven memos each carry an evidence log and a snapshot; the claim logs record Create and Revise events with a unix timestamp and the wording carried at each, so every claim's text as it stood at first render is reconstructible; the evidence logs are in-toto statements whose subject is a claim id and whose predicate carries a verdict. Across all seven, 786 rows break down as 578 supports, 185 qualifies and 23 refutes — so the target set is the 208 non-supporting verdicts, and the measurement is: for each, was that claim's first-render wording one the verifier flags, and does the flag name the same defect the verdict named. The denominators are known before the test runs, which is what makes a kill threshold statable in advance rather than negotiated afterwards.

Two results kill the feature, and both must be declared before the test is run. First, low recall against the verdicts that cost a round: if the verifier surfaces fewer than a quarter of the 23 refutes on their first-render wording, it does not catch the findings that force a revision round, and the whole cost argument — that warning earlier removes a grounding round — fails on the only corpus that could show it. Second, false-positive load: if the verifier flags more than one in ten of the 578 supporting claims at their first-render wording, it is a steering hazard, since the recipient is usually an agent that will act on a warning and each such flag is an invitation to damage a claim that was already sound. Either result kills it regardless of how the other lands, and a run that is merely disappointing on `qualifies` — the largest bucket at 185 — is not a kill, because a qualification is often a legitimate scope narrowing rather than a defect.

The register that keeps a warning from reading as a refusal should ride in a per-finding `guidance` string, not only in the tool description. The precedent already does both: each `attention` entry carries a `guidance` value built beside the finding, and the surrounding tool descriptions set the tone in the same words — "It is not an error — read it and decide". Putting the sentence in the finding itself means it reaches a caller that never re-read the tool description, and it lands inside `fact_result`, the one builder this design already modifies, rather than requiring a separate edit that could drift from the payload. The `attention` precedent additionally shares its advice text verbatim with the CLI so the two surfaces cannot say different things about the same finding, and the `verify` guidance should be produced the same way.

The independence argument that rescued `Domain ⊆ Extent` transfers to a semantic mint-time verifier. `scope.rs` records that the comparison was abandoned as vacuous because one author supplying both sides produced byte-identical results about 80% of the time — "Independence, not capture, was what moved that number" — and that what fixed it was making one side captured by the tool (extent, with deliberately no flag to type one in) and the other authored (the note). A claim's proposition is authored by the same hand; its cited facts' captured output was recorded by `look`/`run` under the same no-typed-input rule. So the two sides of a proposition-versus-captured-output comparison are independent by the same construction, not by the author's diligence.
why: Reading P2 against this claim in `review` showed the paragraph spending the ~80% byte-identical figure, which F2 captured but this claim did not carry. Pulling the number into the claim rather than cutting it from the prose, since it is the measurement the abandonment rested on.

prop: The retrodiction test is runnable today on a corpus already on disk, but its populations are claims and not evidence rows, and the two differ by a factor large enough to change every ratio. Seven memos each carry an evidence log and a snapshot; the claim logs record Create and Revise events with a unix timestamp and the wording carried at each, so a claim's text as it stood at first render is reconstructible whenever the claim existed at first render; the evidence logs are in-toto statements whose subject is a claim id and whose predicate carries a verdict. The row counts are 578 supports, 185 qualifies and 23 refutes over 786 rows, and F13 is right about them — but the test iterates per claim, running the verifier once over one claim's first-render wording and producing at most one flag, so a row count can never be its denominator. Resolved onto claims, those 786 rows cover 143 distinct claims, of which 125 were created at or before their memo's first evidence row and therefore possess a first-render wording at all. The three populations the test can iterate are therefore: 62 claims carrying supports and nothing else, 9 claims carrying at least one refutes, and 60 carrying at least one qualifies. Claims created after first render — 18 of the 143, including 5 of the 14 ever refuted — have no input the test can supply and are excluded from every denominator rather than scored as misses, the same discipline the eval applied to its own errored rows. The measurement per claim is: did the verifier flag that claim's first-render wording, and did the flag name the same defect some later verdict named.
why: Answering the `qualifies` verdict on C17: the row counts are right, but the measurement C17 specifies runs once per claim, and 578/185/23 are row counts standing in a 4.25x multiplicity to claims. Restated over the population the test iterates — distinct claims possessing a first-render wording — using the recount minted as F14, and stating the numerator's unit (one flag per claim) and the rule for claims with no first-render wording (excluded, not scored as misses).

prop: Two results kill the feature, both declared before the test runs, and both are stated over distinct claims possessing a first-render wording, because that is the unit the test iterates and produces at most one flag for. False-positive load: of the 62 claims that carry supports and nothing else anywhere in the corpus, more than one in ten flagged — 7 or more — kills it, since the recipient is usually an agent that acts on a warning and each flag is an invitation to damage a claim that was already sound. Stated this way the gate is trippable in the direction that matters: flagging every one of the 62 scores 100% against a 10% line, where the same numerator over the 578 supports ROWS would have scored 12.1% and an 81% false-positive rate would have passed at 9.9%. Recall: of the 9 claims that were refuted by some later pass and existed at first render, fewer than a quarter — 2 or fewer — flagged with a finding naming the same defect kills it, because the cost argument is that warning earlier removes a revision round. This denominator is 9, so one claim moves it by 11 points: clearing it is not evidence the feature works, only the absence of evidence that it does not, and no threshold on this corpus can be a licence to build. A disappointing showing on the 60 claims carrying a qualifies is not a kill, because a qualification is often a legitimate scope narrowing rather than a defect the author should have avoided, and treating that bucket as the target would reward a verifier that flags everything. Either kill result stands regardless of how the other lands.
why: Answering the `refutes` verdict on C18: both thresholds were ratios of a per-claim numerator to a per-row denominator, which made the false-positive gate nearly untrippable (flagging all 70 sound claims scored 12.1%, and an 81% false-positive rate passed at 9.9%) and gave the recall gate an unknown ceiling. Restated over the populations F14 counts — 62 sound claims and 9 refuted claims that possess a first-render wording — so that each gate's numerator and denominator are the same kind of thing and 100% false positives fails by a factor of ten rather than by two tenths of a point.

prop: The modification surface is larger than one builder, and the reason is that MCP mint results are assembled at three unshared sites rather than one. `fact_result` has exactly one definition and two production call sites, both in src/mcp.rs — the "minted" and "revised" arms — so it covers both `fact` outcomes and no other production caller; its only other occurrences in the worktree are a same-named local binding in a test. It does not cover `claim`. A `claim` result is built by inline `json!` literals in the three `ClaimOutcome` match arms at src/mcp.rs:700, 709 and 710, and `fact_result` appears nowhere in that census; `prose` is built the same way in the three `ProseOutcome` arms at src/mcp.rs:821, 822 and 823. Since `claim` is the verb this design turns on by default, adding a `verify` key to `fact_result` alone would leave the default path untouched. The design therefore names five modification targets, not three: `fact_result`, `ClaimOutcome` and `ProseOutcome` for the three construction sites, plus a new `verify_block` helper — censused at zero occurrences in the worktree, so the name is free — which every site calls so that status, model, `deterministic: false` and guidance cannot drift between verbs. The config work stays self-contained: `known_keys` occurs twice in the whole worktree, both inside src/config.rs, and `Accepts` six times, likewise all inside it with a single variant in use, so the `verify.*` keys mean new registry entries, new `Accepts` variants and matching arms in `accepted` and its message formatter, with no consumer outside that module. The same censuses show `ClaimOutcome` and `ProseOutcome` are also matched by the CLI in src/main.rs, which this design does not modify: the finding is an MCP result field, and the CLI surfaces stay as they are.
why: Answering the `refutes` verdict on C14: the census was accurate but incomplete — a `claim` result is built by inline `json!` literals in the `ClaimOutcome` arms of src/mcp.rs and never touches `fact_result`, so the censused surface omitted the one verb C13 turns on by default, and `prose` is a third unshared site. Re-censused as F15 and restated: three construction sites, a shared `verify_block` builder that does not exist yet, and three further modification targets.

prop: The register that keeps a warning from reading as a refusal should ride in a per-finding `guidance` string, not only in the tool description, and the drift risk that argument raises has to be answered by a shared builder rather than by a coincidence of code layout. The precedent does both: each `attention` entry carries a `guidance` value built beside the finding, and the surrounding tool descriptions set the tone in the same words — "It is not an error — read it and decide" — so putting the sentence in the finding reaches a caller that never re-read a description it loaded once. What cannot be claimed is that this rides along for free inside a single builder. `fact_result` builds only the two `fact` results; the `claim` results are assembled by inline `json!` literals in the `ClaimOutcome` arms at src/mcp.rs:700, 709 and 710, and the `prose` results likewise in the `ProseOutcome` arms at 821, 822 and 823 — three unshared sites, of which the default-on verb is not the one `fact_result` reaches. So `verify` must be added at each site explicitly, and the guidance string, the status vocabulary and the `deterministic: false` marker must all be produced by one shared `verify_block` helper rather than restated per site. That is the same discipline `attention` already applies by sharing its advice text verbatim with the CLI so two surfaces cannot say different things about one finding.
why: Answering the `refutes` verdict on C19: the guidance-in-the-payload argument survives but its stated reason ("lands inside `fact_result`, rather than requiring a separate edit that could drift") is false for `claim`, the default-on verb, whose result is built inline and never calls `fact_result`. Replaced that reason with the remedy the census supports — one shared `verify_block` builder called at all three sites, with the guidance text a single shared constant, the way `advice` is shared with the CLI.

prop: Latency is the binding constraint, it is larger than a per-record estimate suggests, and the reply path must therefore contain no provider call at all. The unit paying the cost is the tool call, not the record: in the largest memo on disk (tet47) the append-only logs carry 33 + 114 + 130 = 277 lines across facts, claims and prose, and 114 of those claim lines resolve to only 39 distinct claim ids, so roughly two thirds of claim traffic is revision; at the eval's observed per-call latency, verifying every line costs tens of minutes of added wall-clock while the money stays negligible. Committing the mint before the call is necessary but not sufficient, because a mint result is ONE structured object: `fact_result` carries `attention`, `folded` and `refused_since_previous_fact` in the same payload, and the `claim` result carries `overlap`, all of them deterministic findings that arrive with certainty today only because a mint is instant. Putting a model call in front of that reply makes all of them contingent on the provider — a client whose own request timeout is shorter than `verify.timeout_ms`, or an author who interrupts, loses a note-outside-extent warning that no model was involved in producing. So the design (a) returns the mint result immediately, with `verify` carrying only what can be decided without a call, (b) runs the comparison after the reply and delivers its finding on the author's next authoring call in that workspace, appending it to `verify.log` as well — the pattern `refusals_since_last_mint` already establishes, where a mint reports findings from the window before it, through one helper shared by CLI and MCP so the two cannot drift, (c) bounds the background call with `verify.timeout_ms`, measured per mint across all retries rather than per HTTP attempt, and (d) skips the call entirely when a revision does not change the text being compared, which is where most of the volume is. The cost of (b) is that a warning arrives one tool call later than the writing it concerns; the whole latency budget leaves the author's critical path in exchange, and a finding delivered on the next call is still many rounds earlier than a grounding pass.
why: Answering the `qualifies` verdict on C12: committing the mint before the call protects the record but leaves `attention`, `folded`, `refused_since_previous_fact` and `overlap` riding in the same single structured result as `verify`, so a client timeout shorter than `verify.timeout_ms` discards deterministic findings that have nothing to do with the model. Replaced (a) with a stronger shape the repository already uses — nothing in the reply path waits for the provider at all, and the finding is delivered on the next authoring call in that workspace, the way `refusals_since_last_mint` delivers a previous window's refusals.

prop: The degradation contract is format-level and total only if it includes the state a well-formed HTTP exchange can still land in. Every terminal state of the provider call maps to exactly one `verify.status`: disabled by config gives `off`; no key in the environment gives `unauthorized`; a transport failure or non-2xx gives `unavailable`; expiry of the budget gives `timeout`; an empty or truncated body gives `unavailable`, never `ok`, because the eval measured that state — a draw reaching the token ceiling returns `finish_reason=length` with content of length zero. The state the first drafting of this contract missed is a 2xx reply with a non-empty, non-truncated body that is not a usable answer, and the harness this design copies shows it has three shapes rather than one: `parse` returns no verdict when the body contains no brace-delimited substring at all, when `json.loads` of the substring it finds raises `JSONDecodeError`, and when the decoded object's "verdict" is outside ("supports", "refutes", "qualifies"). All three map to `unparsable`. `ok` is reachable only from a decoded object carrying one of those three verdict values, so no path reaches `ok` with an empty `findings` array except a well-formed answer that genuinely contains no finding — which is what stops this contract reproducing the harness defect it cites, where an errored row recorded as unflagged read as a miss on a defective case and a correct silence on a sound one. The budget's unit is stated with it: `verify.timeout_ms` bounds one mint's verification end to end, covering every retry, not one HTTP attempt — the harness's `ask` retries up to three times with a tripled cap, so a per-attempt bound would let a single mint spend three times its declared budget. Because the call runs after the mint result has already been returned, every one of these states is reported on a later call and none of them can fail a mint, delay a reply or change an exit code.
why: Answering the `refutes` verdict on C15: the mapping was not total. A 2xx response with a non-empty, non-truncated body that carries no usable verdict matched none of the six states and fell through to `ok` with empty findings — the exact "scored an error as an answer" defect the claim cites as its justification. F16 captures the three real shapes of that state in the harness's own `parse`. Added an `unparsable` state covering all three, made `ok` conditional on a decoded verdict from the fixed vocabulary, and pinned the timeout budget's unit, since the same harness retries up to three times with a tripled cap.

prop: The warning should be carried as a top-level `verify` OBJECT in the mint result, not a fourth array beside `attention` and `overlap`. `mcp.rs` establishes the array form for a reason that holds here — "the caller is a program, and a field it can branch on beats a string it has to notice" — but `attention` and `overlap` are derived per call from workspace state already on disk, so empty and absent mean the same thing for them. A verification can be switched off, refused for want of a key, fail in transport, time out, or come back unreadable, and in every one of those states "found nothing" is a different fact from "did not look"; on top of that the call runs after the reply it was triggered by, so the result that starts a verification can never report its outcome. Only an object can carry both halves. `verify` therefore has a mandatory `status` field with a fixed vocabulary: the reply that triggers a verification reports `off`, `unauthorized` or `queued`, all decidable without a call, and the reply that delivers one reports `ok`, `unavailable`, `timeout` or `unparsable`, together with the id of the mint the findings concern, since it is no longer the id in the same result. `findings` is meaningful only under `ok`. A caller that branches on `verify.status` cannot mistake a silent outage, a disabled feature or an in-flight call for a clean bill; a bare array can express none of these.
why: Not graded, but the deferred-delivery shape adopted in C12 changes what the `verify` object must be able to say: the reply that triggers a verification cannot report that verification's outcome. Extending the status vocabulary with `queued` (and `unparsable`, from C15) and naming which id a delivered batch concerns, so a caller can still branch on every state.

prop: Requiring a finding to quote the evidence is worthless unless the quotation is checked, because a fabricated quotation is strictly worse than a bare verdict: it directs a recipient to check against text that does not exist, and the checking step the quotation was introduced to invite is the step that fails. The model's answer is free text — the harness recovers a verdict from it with a regular expression and `json.loads`, and nothing in that path constrains what appears inside the JSON — so a quoted span in a finding is an unconstrained string the model produced, not evidence. This repository already owns the mechanism that fixes it. `Fact::quotes` decides whether a string is a verbatim substring of a SINGLE observation's captured output, byte for byte with no normalisation of whitespace, comment prefixes or line endings, and single rather than joined so a span straddling two observations cannot be assembled from text that was never contiguous; it is a plain `contains` over captured output, with no model, no network and no knowledge of the donor's language, and it is what makes `transplant` refuse a premise that is not the donor's own words. The same call decides each finding's quoted span before that finding is put in the payload: a span `quotes` accepts ships as a quotation, and a span it rejects is dropped and its finding downgraded to one that carries no evidence quotation at all and is labelled as such. This is deterministic, costs one substring search, and applies to the model's output rather than to the author's — so it neither refuses a mint nor suppresses a finding, it only withholds the authority a quotation carries from text that did not come from the captured record.

The independence argument that rescued `Domain ⊆ Extent` transfers to a semantic mint-time verifier only if both of its properties are carried across, and carrying the second one is a design decision this memo has to make rather than inherit. `scope.rs` records that the comparison was abandoned as vacuous because one author supplying both sides produced byte-identical results about 80% of the time — "Independence, not capture, was what moved that number" — and that what fixed it was making one side captured by the tool, extent, "with deliberately no flag to type one in", against an authored note. That construction has two halves: the captured side cannot be TYPED, and it is COMPLETE, because `look` and `run` record what was actually opened. For a claim the first half survives untouched — an author cannot type the captured output of a cited fact. The second does not survive by itself: the captured side would be the output of the facts the author CHOSE to cite, and an author with an overreaching proposition could cite only the facts consistent with it, leaving the verifier to see no disagreement because the disagreeing evidence was filtered out before the comparison. tetel already treats that choice as unreliable, which is exactly why creating a claim returns an overlap report of facts touching the same files that the author did NOT cite. Both are on disk at claim time and neither costs a new mechanism: `overlap_report` runs inside `create`, one line before the claim event is appended, having loaded every fact in the workspace to compute it. With that union as the captured side, neither half of the comparison can be typed and neither can be narrowed by selection, and the two sides are independent by construction rather than by the author's diligence.

Rather than narrowing the claim to "cannot be typed, but can be narrowed by selection", the design now takes the remedy the verdict names: the comparison runs against the cited facts UNION the overlap set, which F19 shows is computed at claim time from facts already on disk. That restores completeness and makes the transfer whole.

prop: Shipping this falsifies one of `lib.rs`'s two pinned whole-crate properties, and the correct replacement is a per-command row rather than a weakened sentence — which is what the module's own preamble already prescribes, having recorded that "a single sentence about the whole crate was wrong for months" and having restated the write list per command for exactly that reason. The property that breaks is "there are no network calls anywhere, which the dependency set enforces rather than the prose": once an HTTP client is linked, the dependency set no longer enforces anything and the sentence would be prose pretending to be an invariant. The replacement must cover every command the file lists, all fifteen of them, or it reintroduces the same defect through the enumeration instead of the generalisation. Three reach: `fact`, `claim` and `prose` may make one outbound call to the configured provider, and only when enabled with a key in the environment. Eleven make none — `check`, `brief`, `query`, `review`, `workspaces`, `look`, `target`, `transplant`, `render`, `record` and `config`. The fifteenth is `run`, which needs its own line rather than membership in either list: this crate makes no call of its own for `run`, but `run` spawns the command the AUTHOR typed, in the author's own session, and that process may reach the network exactly as any command the author runs in a terminal may. That distinction was invisible while the property was categorical and about the crate's own calls; a per-command row has to state it. The crate's other pinned property, that nothing here ever executes a command named by a document, is untouched — `run` executes what the author types, never what a memo contains — and it is the reason `check` must not be a reaching command.
why: Answering the `qualifies` verdict on C9: the replacement enumerated 11 of the 15 commands `lib.rs` lists, leaving `look`, `run`, `target` and `transplant` with nothing said about them — the same drift the preamble records, arriving through the enumeration rather than the generalisation. All fifteen are now named, and `run` gets its own line: the crate makes no call for it, but it spawns a process the author typed, which can reach the network itself.

For a claim the first half survives untouched — an author cannot type the captured output of a cited fact. prop: A workspace-local `verify.log` beside `refusals.log` is the right place for findings to persist, but `refusals.log` is the wrong sibling to imitate in one specific respect: it is an entry in SNAPSHOT_FILES and therefore ships into `<memo>.tetel/` with every render. A log of model output that shipped that way would put non-reproducible text into the snapshot, which is the one thing this design must not do. What makes the omission safe is that SNAPSHOT_FILES is an enumerated allowlist of ten names rather than a denylist, and `write` iterates exactly that array — `for name in SNAPSHOT_FILES { let src = workspace_dir.join(name); if src.exists() { fs::copy(&src, dir.join(name))?; } }` — so a workspace file whose name is not in the array cannot be copied at all. The array's doc comment states that as its purpose: "Enumerated rather than copied wholesale so that a future workspace file is a deliberate decision to ship or withhold, not an accident of `cp -r`." It is the enumeration that does the enforcing, and not a commenting convention: only four of the ten entries — targets.jsonl, transplants.jsonl, identity.json and acks.jsonl — carry a justifying comment beside them, and of the six that do not, only pending.json is argued for in the array's own doc comment. So shipping a new file takes a deliberate line in that array, while withholding one takes nothing: `verify.log` is enforced out of the snapshot by construction rather than by a promise, and its absence needs no new mechanism.
why: Answering the C11 qualification: the commenting convention asserted is not the file's practice — four of the ten SNAPSHOT_FILES entries carry a comment, and five have no justification anywhere. F22 re-opens the array and `write`. The clause is replaced with what actually enforces the withholding: the enumeration, plus `write` copying only names drawn from it.

prop: Two results kill the feature, both declared before the test runs, and both are stated over distinct claims possessing a first-render wording, because that is the unit the test iterates and produces at most one flag for. False-positive load: of the 62 claims that carry supports and nothing else anywhere in the corpus, more than one in ten flagged — 7 or more, since 7/62 is 11.3% where 6/62 is 9.7% — kills it, since the recipient is usually an agent that acts on a warning and each flag is an invitation to damage a claim that was already sound. Stated this way the gate is trippable in the direction that matters, where a gate stated over rows is very nearly not: flagging every one of the 62 scores 100% against a 10% line, whereas the same numerator over the corpus's 578 supports ROWS would have scored 10.7%, and an 81% false-positive rate — 50 of the 62 — would have passed at 8.7%. (Of those 578 rows, 510 belong to the 125 claims that have a first-render wording at all; over 510 the same two numerators give 12.2% and 9.8%, so the near-untrippability is a property of using a row count as the denominator and not of which row count is chosen.) Recall: of the 9 claims that were refuted by some later pass and existed at first render, fewer than a quarter — 2 or fewer — flagged with a finding naming the same defect kills it, because the cost argument is that warning earlier removes a revision round. This denominator is 9, so one claim moves it by 11 points: clearing it is not evidence the feature works, only the absence of evidence that it does not, and no threshold on this corpus can be a licence to build. A disappointing showing on the 60 claims carrying a qualifies is not a kill, because a qualification is often a legitimate scope narrowing rather than a defect the author should have avoided, and treating that bucket as the target would reward a verifier that flags everything. Either kill result stands regardless of how the other lands.
why: Answering the C18 qualification: the two illustrative percentages were computed against 510 (the supports rows belonging to first-render claims) while the sentence names 578. F21 recomputes both against the denominator the sentence actually names — 10.7% and 8.7% — which is the honest fix, since the illustration's point survives at those figures. The gate itself is unchanged.

prop: The register that keeps a warning from reading as a refusal should ride in a per-finding `guidance` string, not only in the tool description, and the drift risk that argument raises has to be answered by a shared builder rather than by a coincidence of code layout. The precedent carries the register in both places, but not in the same words, and the split is the argument rather than a blemish on it. In the payload: each `attention` entry carries a `guidance` value built beside the finding from `scope::advice`, whose own text hedges in its own terms — "Fine if that's context. If it's a conclusion about {}, you have not read it here". In the description: the sentence "It is not an error — read it and decide" belongs to the `claim` tool's description and is about the OVERLAP report; it is not `attention`'s text and does not appear in `advice`'s output. So the sharpest statement of the register sits on a surface a caller loads once and may never re-read, while the finding that needs it travels alone — which is the reason to put a register string in the finding itself rather than to rely on the description. What cannot be claimed is that this rides along for free inside a single builder. `fact_result` builds only the two `fact` results; the `claim` results are assembled by inline `json!` literals in the `ClaimOutcome` arms at src/mcp.rs:700, 709 and 710, and the `prose` results likewise in the `ProseOutcome` arms at 821, 822 and 823 — three unshared sites, of which the default-on verb is not the one `fact_result` reaches. So `verify` must be added at each site explicitly, and the guidance string, the status vocabulary and the `deterministic: false` marker must all be produced by one shared `verify_block` helper rather than restated per site. That is the same discipline `scope::advice` already enforces for `attention`, its single definition reaching both the MCP payload at src/mcp.rs:185 and the CLI at src/main.rs:650 and :657, so two surfaces cannot say different things about one finding.
why: Answering the C19 qualification: "It is not an error — read it and decide" is the `claim` tool description's sentence about the overlap report, not `attention`'s and not `scope::advice`'s. F24 censuses where the register actually lives. Attribution corrected, and the correction is folded into the argument rather than dropped, since a sentence living only in a description is precisely the case for putting the register in the payload.

prop: Only `claim` should be checked by default, with `fact` and `prose` available through `verify.verbs` but off — and the reason cannot be that `claim` is the only verb the eval measured, because it is not. The 15-case set is two files mixed: the 12 in-scope cases of `cases.py` plus the 3 of `extra_cases.py`, whose docstring says they are "Cases aimed at the note-versus-extent check specifically" — that is the `fact` mint comparison — and every harness assembles its run as `cases = [c for c in CASES if c.get("scope", "in") == "in"] + EXTRA_CASES`. So 2 of each run's 11 defective cases and 1 of its 4 sound ones are `fact` cases, the headline 32/33 and 12/12 are summed over both verbs, and the harness emits no per-verb column. That cuts against a per-verb argument in both directions: `fact` does have measured numbers, and `claim`'s cannot be separated from them, so the eval licenses no statement about either verb's accuracy on its own — which is a further reason for caution about the columns, not a reason to prefer one verb. The default set is therefore decided on existing coverage and on volume, not on measured accuracy. `claim` is the comparison nothing in the crate performs today: the deterministic findings that exist are `attention`, a note against its own extent, and `overlap`, which by design carries fact ids and shared extent keys and explicitly "not that fact's note", so no current check reads a proposition against the content of the evidence cited for it. `fact` is the one verb whose comparison is already half done, deterministically and for free, by the `scope` check — and the size of the semantic residue is unmeasured, so this design does not assert one: `scope.rs`'s only datum is that it catches one of the two overreaches that motivated it, which suggests parity rather than a smaller half, and `extra_cases.py`'s docstring records the deterministic check as weak in its own terms, catching a note that names an unopened file "only when the file's name happens not to appear anywhere in the extent string". `fact` stays off because it is partly covered and would spend budget on a residue nobody has sized, and it is the first verb to turn on if the residue is later measured. `prose` is the highest-volume verb of the three in the largest memo measured (130 log lines against 114 for claims and 33 for facts), and comparing prose against claim propositions is a comparison neither case file contains, with no numbers behind it at all. Defaulting it on would spend the largest share of the latency budget on the least-evidenced comparison.
why: Answering the C13 qualification, whose first clause was inherited from a false premise: the eval DID measure `fact`. F20 opens extra_cases.py and the harnesses' run assembly and shows the 15-case set is 12 claim-shaped plus 3 note-versus-extent cases, mixed into one headline. The default-on decision is therefore re-argued from coverage and volume instead of from a measured-verb distinction that does not exist, and the unsupported "smaller of the two halves" size comparison is dropped for what scope.rs and extra_cases.py actually say.

prop: The verifier's settings may be added to `config.rs` only if each is visible in the output it affects, which is the module's own stated admission test and is stated with a consequence: "every setting here must be visible in the output it affects ... A setting that could not be shown that way should not be added to this file." Five keys are wanted — `verify.enabled` (bool), `verify.model` (string), `verify.approach` (direct or pipeline), `verify.timeout_ms` (int) and `verify.verbs` (which mint verbs are checked) — and a `verify` object echoing only status, model name and the non-determinism marker would fail that test for three of them: `verify.approach` would appear nowhere in the response shape, so a reader could not tell which of two materially different mechanisms produced the finding in front of them; `verify.timeout_ms` would be visible only in the single terminal state that trips it; and `verify.verbs` only by inference from an absence. The design answers that by widening the echo rather than by keeping a key that fails the rule it quotes: the shared `verify_block` helper puts the EFFECTIVE value of all five into every `verify` object it builds — `status` (which reports `off` when `verify.enabled` is false), `model`, `approach`, `timeout_ms` and `verbs` — alongside `deterministic: false`. Each of the five is then on the page of every response, including the responses where the setting made nothing happen, which is what the admission test asks for and what a reader needs in order to tell which settings produced the result in front of them without opening a config file. With the echo widened, the five are each one entry in the existing static KEYS registry with an `accepts` rule, live at the two existing scopes, and need no third scope. One caveat about the evidence rather than about the design: `src/config.rs` is untracked at the pinned HEAD, so every observation here is true of the working tree at that commit, taken by a filesystem `look` rather than by any search of the committed tree.
why: Answering the C8 qualification: under config.rs's own admission test, an echo of status/model/determinism leaves `verify.approach` invisible in the output it affects, and `timeout_ms` and `verbs` nearly so — the rule the design quotes to justify its placement says such a key should not be added. Rather than drop a key the design needs, the echo is widened so `verify_block` emits all five effective values in every response. F25 also records that src/config.rs is untracked at the pinned HEAD and which search reached it.

prop: The gate has been run, and it returned a split verdict rather than a pass: the steering-hazard line passes with 4 of the 62 supports-only claims flagged against a kill at 7 or more, and the recall line fires with 2 of the 9 ever-refuted claims carrying a finding that names the defect a later pass named, against a kill at 2 or fewer. Three of the nine were flagged; the third flag, on tet61's C15, is a correct arithmetic finding about a census, which is not the defect either of that claim's refutations named, so it counts on the flag column and not on the naming one.

What the fired line establishes is bounded by what it counted. It counted claims a later pass refuted — nine of them with a first-render wording — and the verifier named the defect on two. That is the measurement the cost argument needed and did not clear, and the cost argument is therefore withdrawn from this design rather than defended. It is not a measurement of the warning's worth to the author receiving it, and the same run carries that number too: 23 of the 125 claims were flagged, 19 of them claims a later pass did not simply support, so four flags across the whole corpus land on a claim that was already sound. The feature is built on that second reading — a cheap, precise, non-blocking finding delivered where the fix costs one re-look — and no longer on the claim that it removes a grounding round.

The population this corpus cannot settle is its largest: 18 of the 60 claims carrying at least one qualifies were flagged, and the gate declined in advance to make that bucket a kill condition on the ground that a qualification is frequently a legitimate narrowing of scope rather than a defect the author should have avoided. Those 18 are therefore unresolved by construction — the corpus cannot say whether they are findings a grader would have welcomed at mint time or noise an agent would have acted on — and no re-run of this data can resolve them, because the ground truth it would need is the thing the corpus lacks. The measurement that settles it is recording the verifier's flags beside the graders' verdicts on memos written after it ships, which is a reason to instrument the feature from its first day rather than a reason to hold it.

why: The grounding pass found that errored draws are not excluded from the denominators, contrary to what the tally script's docstring claimed. Three claims were never actually answered and are scored as unflagged. It does not change a number, but a gate result that does not say which of its denominators contain an unasked question is overstating its own precision.
